subject: physics
stem: In a Vernier calipers, when both jaws touch each other, zero of the Vernier scale is shifted to the right of zero of the main scale and $7^{\text{th}}$ Vernier division coincides with a main scale reading. If the value of 1 main scale division is 1 mm and there are 10 Vernier scale divisions, then the Vernier caliper has _______.

steps.text: 10 Vernier divisions coincide with 9 main-scale divisions, so $1\,\text{VSD} = 0.9$ mm and the least count is $\text{LC} = 1\,\text{mm} - 0.9\,\text{mm} = 0.1$ mm.
With jaws closed, the $7^{\text{th}}$ Vernier division coincides, so the zero error magnitude is $7 \times 0.1\,\text{mm} = 0.7\,\text{mm} = 0.07\,\text{cm}$.
Zero of the Vernier lies to the right of (ahead of) the main-scale zero, so the instrument reads a positive value when the true reading is zero: the zero error is positive.
Hence the caliper has $0.07$ cm positive zero error.

pitfalls: Mixing up positive vs negative zero error: Vernier zero ahead (right) of main zero means positive error.
Forgetting to convert mm to cm: $0.7$ mm $= 0.07$ cm, not $0.7$ cm.
solution.final_check: LC $= 0.1$ mm, $7 \times$ LC $= 0.7$ mm $= 0.07$ cm, and right-shifted Vernier zero gives positive error: option (C).

subject: physics
stem: $L$, $C$ and $R$ represent the physical quantities inductance, capacitance and resistance respectively. The dimensional formula $\mathrm{M\,L^2\,T^{-4}\,A^{-2}}$ corresponds to _______.

steps.text: The other options give $\mathrm{ML^2T^{-5}A^{-2}}$, $\mathrm{M^{-2}L^{-3}T^{5}A^{3}}$, $\mathrm{M^{-2}L^{-3}T^{3}A^{2}}$ respectively, so only (A) works.

pitfalls: Using $[C] = \mathrm{M^{-1}L^{-2}T^{2}A^{2}}$ (missing $T^4$) is the most common slip.
Note $[LC] = T^2$ since $1/\sqrt{LC}$ is the natural frequency of an LC circuit.
solution.final_check: $[R]/\sqrt{[LC]} = \mathrm{ML^2T^{-3}A^{-2}}/\mathrm{T} = \mathrm{ML^2T^{-4}A^{-2}}$: option (A).

subject: physics
stem: When one moves from a point 16 km below the earth's surface to a point 16 km above the earth's surface, the change in $g$ is approximately $\alpha$\%. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.\n(Take radius of the earth $= 6400$ km.)

concepts: Variation of g with depth and height
pitfalls: Using $g_h = g(1 - h/R)$ instead of $g(1 - 2h/R)$ for height (the factor 2 comes from the inverse-square law).
Forgetting that going up decreases $g$ twice as fast (per km) as going down.

subject: physics
stem: Three masses $m_1 = 4$ kg, $m_2 = 4$ kg and $m_3 = 6$ kg are suspended from a fixed smooth frictionless pulley as shown in the figure below. The value of $T_1/T_2$ is _______.\n(take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)\n[Figure: a fixed pulley; mass $m_1$ hangs from the left string (tension $T_1$); on the right, mass $m_2$ hangs from the main string (tension $T_1$ above it) and mass $m_3$ is suspended below $m_2$ by a second string of tension $T_2$.]

steps.text: The right side ($m_2 + m_3 = 10$ kg) is heavier, so it descends with $a = \dfrac{(10 - 4)g}{10 + 4} = \dfrac{6g}{14} = \dfrac{3g}{7}$.
For $m_1$ (rising): $T_1 - m_1 g = m_1 a$, so $T_1 = 4\left(g + \dfrac{3g}{7}\right) = \dfrac{40g}{7}$.
For $m_3$ (descending with the right side): $m_3 g - T_2 = m_3 a$, so $T_2 = 6\left(g - \dfrac{3g}{7}\right) = \dfrac{24g}{7}$.

pitfalls: Treating $m_2$ and $m_3$ as separate sides of the pulley instead of one combined 10 kg mass.
Using $T_2 = m_3 g$ (static) instead of $m_3(g - a)$.

subject: physics
stem: A wedge $Y$ of mass 10 kg with all frictionless surfaces has its inclined surface making $37^\circ$ with the horizontal. A block $X$ of mass 2 kg is placed at the highest point of the wedge as shown in the figure and is at rest. At $t = 0$ the wedge ($Y$) is pulled toward the right with a constant force $f = 24$ N. Taking the block $X$ to be at rest at $t = 0$, the time taken by it to slide down 8.8 m on the slope, while $Y$ is on the move, is _______ s.\n(take $\tan(37^\circ) = 3/4$ and $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)\n[Figure: a right-triangle wedge $Y$ with a $37^\circ$ incline; block $X$ sits at the top of the incline; a horizontal force $f = 24$ N pulls the wedge to the right.]

steps.text: Wedge acceleration: $a_Y = \dfrac{24}{10} = 2.4$ m/s$^2$ to the right.

In the wedge frame the block feels a pseudo force $m a_Y$ to the left. With $\sin37^\circ = 3/5$, $\cos37^\circ = 4/5$: acceleration of the block down the slope relative to the wedge is $a_{\text{rel}} = g\sin37^\circ - a_Y\cos37^\circ = 10\cdot\tfrac{3}{5} - 2.4\cdot\tfrac{4}{5} = 6 - 1.92 = 4.08$ m/s$^2$.
Among the options, this corresponds to $2$ s.

pitfalls: Getting the pseudo-force direction wrong: the wedge accelerates right, so pseudo acts left, i.e. partly UP the slope (it opposes sliding).
The computed time is $\approx 2.08$ s rather than exactly 2 s; option (A) is the intended/nearest choice.
solution.final_check: $a_{rel} = 4.08$ m/s$^2$ gives $t \approx 2.08$ s, nearest option (A) $2$ s.

subject: physics
stem: The Young's modulus of a steel wire of radius $r$ and length $L$ is $Y$. If the radius $r$ and length $L$ of the wire are doubled, then the value of $Y$ _______.

steps.text: Young's modulus is the ratio of stress to strain for the material; it depends only on the nature of the material (steel), not on the wire's dimensions.
Doubling $r$ quadruples the area and doubling $L$ doubles the extension for the same load, but the ratio $\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$ stays the same.

pitfalls: Confusing the extension $\Delta L$ (which does change) with the modulus $Y$ (which does not).
solution.final_check: $Y$ is a material constant, independent of $r$ and $L$: option (C).

subject: physics
stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R**.
**Assertion A:** Change in internal energy of a system containing $n$ moles of ideal gas can be written as $\Delta U = nC_v(T_f - T_i) = \dfrac{nR}{\gamma - 1}(T_f - T_i)$, where $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v}$, $T_i =$ initial temperature, $T_f =$ final temperature.
**Reason R:** Relation between degree of freedom $f$ and $\gamma$ ($= C_p/C_v$) is $\left(\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f}ight)$.
Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below:

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

formulas: $\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T$ (ideal gas, any process)

steps.text: Assertion A: $\Delta U = nC_v(T_f - T_i)$ holds for an ideal gas in any process. Since $C_p - C_v = R$ and $\gamma = C_p/C_v$, we get $C_v(\gamma - 1) = R$, i.e. $C_v = R/(\gamma-1)$. So $\Delta U = \dfrac{nR}{\gamma-1}(T_f-T_i)$. Assertion is true.
Reason R: from $C_v = fR/2$ and $C_p = C_v + R$, $\gamma = 1 + R/C_v = 1 + 2/f$. Reason is true.

But the step $C_v = R/(\gamma-1)$ uses only Mayer's relation $C_p - C_v = R$ and the definition of $\gamma$; it does not use the $f$-dependence of $\gamma$. So R is true but is NOT the correct explanation of A.

pitfalls: Assuming every true statement about $\gamma$ explains the formula; explanation requires the specific logical link (here Mayer's relation).
solution.final_check: A true via $C_p-C_v=R$; R true via $C_v=fR/2$ but not the reason for A: option (B).

subject: physics
stem:
Consider the following statements:
A. Zeroth law of thermodynamics gives concept of temperature
B. First law of thermodynamics gives concept of internal energy
C. In isothermal expansion of ideal gas, $\Delta Q 
eq \Delta W$
D. Product of intensive and extensive variables is extensive
E. The ratio of any extensive variable to mass will be an extensive variable
Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below:

formulas: Isothermal ideal gas: $\Delta U = 0 \Rightarrow \Delta Q = \Delta W$

steps.text: A: Zeroth law defines thermal equilibrium and hence temperature. True.
B: First law ($\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$) introduces internal energy $U$ as a state function. True.
C: For isothermal expansion of an ideal gas $\Delta U = 0$, so $\Delta Q = \Delta W$; the claim $\Delta Q \neq \Delta W$ is false.
D: (intensive) $\times$ (extensive) is extensive (e.g. pressure $\times$ volume). True.
E: extensive/mass is a specific (intensive) quantity, e.g. density; not extensive. False.
True statements: A, B, D only.

pitfalls: Statement E is the classic trap: dividing by mass always gives an intensive (specific) variable.
Statement C: sign conventions aside, $|\Delta Q| = |\Delta W|$ for isothermal ideal gas.
solution.final_check: A, B, D true; C, E false: option (C).

subject: physics
stem: Refer to the figure given below. The values of $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$ are _______.\n[Figure: a diamond (bridge) circuit with top vertex T and bottom vertex B. Top-left edge: $4\,\Omega$; bottom-left edge: $4\,\Omega$ carrying $I_3$ from the left vertex L to B. Middle vertical branch T-B: two $2\,\Omega$ resistors in series with midpoint M. Horizontal branch L-M: a 10 V battery (positive terminal toward L) in series with $1\,\Omega$, carrying $I_1$ from M toward L. Right branch T-B: a wire carrying $I_2$ upward (toward T) in series with a 5 V battery (positive terminal toward T).]

formulas: KCL: $\sum I_{\text{in}} = \sum I_{\text{out}}$ at each node

steps.text: The 5 V battery fixes $V_T - V_B = 5$ V. Set $V_B = 0$, so $V_T = 5$ V.

KCL at M: $\dfrac{V_M - V_T}{2} + \dfrac{V_M}{2} + I_1 = 0$, and along L-M (traversed M to L): $V_M - V_L = I_1(1) - 10$ (battery $+$ toward L). So $I_1 = \tfrac{V_T}{2} - V_M$ and $2V_M - V_L = \tfrac{V_T}{2} - 10$.
KCL at L: $\dfrac{V_L}{4} + \dfrac{V_L - V_T}{4} = I_1$, giving $V_L + 2V_M = \tfrac{3}{2}V_T$.
Then $I_3 = V_L/4 = 1.875$ A (L to B); $I_1 = 2.5 - V_M = 2.5$ A (M to L); KCL at T gives $I_2 = \dfrac{V_T - V_L}{4} + \dfrac{V_T - V_M}{2} = \dfrac{3V_T}{8} = 1.875$ A (upward).

pitfalls: Battery polarity decides everything here: the 10 V source has $+$ toward L and the 5 V source has $+$ toward T; reversing either changes all three currents.
Do not assume the bridge is balanced (here $V_M = 0 \neq V_L$).
solution.final_check: Nodal check: $V_T=5, V_M=0, V_L=7.5$ satisfies KCL at T, L, M: option (A).

subject: physics
stem: An electron of mass $m$ is moving in an electric field $\vec{E} = -2E_0\hat{i}$ ($E_0 =$ constant $> 0$), with an initial velocity $\vec{V} = v_0\hat{j}$ ($v_0 =$ constant $> 0$). If $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{h}{4mv_0}$, its de Broglie wavelength at time $t$ is _______.\n($e =$ charge of electron)

steps.text: Momentum gained from the field in time $t$: $\Delta p = 2eE_0 t$. Initial momentum $p_0 = mv_0$.
Total momentum (in the form the options use): $p = mv_0 + 2eE_0 t$.
Since $\lambda_0 = h/(4mv_0)$, i.e. $h = 4\lambda_0 m v_0$: $\lambda = \dfrac{4\lambda_0 m v_0}{mv_0 + 2eE_0 t} = \dfrac{4\lambda_0}{1 + \dfrac{2E_0 e}{m}\dfrac{t}{v_0}}$.
The wavelength decreases with time (electron speeds up), so the $+$ sign options are the candidates, and the field $2E_0$ fixes the coefficient $2E_0e/m$: option (C).

pitfalls: The field is $2E_0$, not $E_0$: options (A)/(B) with $E_0e/2m$ correspond to misreading the field.
Since the electron accelerates, $\lambda$ must decrease: options with $-$ in the denominator are unphysical here.

Note: this derivation adds the field-gained momentum collinearly with the initial momentum, which is the form the options demand; the exact vector treatment gives $\lambda = 4\lambda_0/\sqrt{1 + (2eE_0t/mv_0)^2}$.
solution.final_check: At $t=0$, $\lambda = 4\lambda_0 = h/mv_0$ ✓; $\lambda$ falls as $t$ grows: option (C).

subject: physics
stem: In the hydrogen atom, the electron makes a transition from a higher orbit ($i$) to a lower orbit ($f$). The ratio of the radii of the orbits is given by $r_i : r_f = 16 : 4$. The wavelength of the photon emitted due to this transition is _______ nm.\n(Given Rydberg constant $= 1.0973 \times 10^7$/m)

steps.text: $r_n \propto n^2$, so $\dfrac{n_i^2}{n_f^2} = \dfrac{16}{4} = 4$, giving $n_i : n_f = 4 : 2$. The transition is $4 \to 2$ (Balmer $H_\beta$).

pitfalls: Taking $n_i : n_f = 16:4$ directly (forgetting $r \propto n^2$); the ratio of $n$ is the square root, $4:2$.
solution.final_check: $4\to2$ Balmer line: $\lambda = 16/3R \approx 486$ nm: option (C).

subject: physics
stem: A displacement current of 4.0 A can be set up in the space between two parallel plates of a $6\,\mu$F capacitor. The rate of change of potential difference across the plates of the capacitor is nearly $\alpha \times 10^6$ V/s. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.

steps.text: Displacement current equals the rate of change of charge on the plates: $I_d = C\,dV/dt$.

pitfalls: Using $I_d = \epsilon_0 d\Phi_E/dt$ directly without converting to $C\,dV/dt$; both work but $C\,dV/dt$ is immediate.
Unit slip: $6\,\mu$F $= 6\times10^{-6}$ F.

subject: physics
stem: Refer to the figure given below. Current between terminals $A$ and $B$ is _______ A.\n[Figure: three identical rows connected in parallel between A (left) and B (right). Each row consists of three 5 V batteries (each with $+$ on the left) alternating with three $3\,\Omega$ resistors: $+5$V$\,-$ $3\Omega$ $+5$V$\,-$ $3\Omega$ $+5$V$\,-$ $3\Omega$. A fourth branch directly between A and B consists of three $3\,\Omega$ resistors in series.]

formulas: Series aiding: $E_{eq} = nE$, $r_{eq} = nr$; parallel identical: $E_{eq} = E$, $r_{eq} = r/n$

steps.text: Each of the three upper rows: three 5 V cells aiding in series give $E = 15$ V with internal resistance $3 \times 3 = 9\,\Omega$.
Three such identical rows in parallel: equivalent source $E_{eq} = 15$ V, $r_{eq} = 9/3 = 3\,\Omega$.
The branch directly between A and B is $3 + 3 + 3 = 9\,\Omega$ (the load).

pitfalls: Adding EMFs of parallel rows (voltage stays 15 V; only internal resistance divides by 3).
Reading the bottom $3+3+3\,\Omega$ as a short (it is a $9\,\Omega$ load, not a wire).
solution.final_check: Thevenin $15$ V, $3\,\Omega$ into $9\,\Omega$: $15/12 = 1.25$ A: option (B).

subject: physics
stem: In Young's double slit experiment, the fringe width of the interference pattern produced on the screen is $2.4\,\mu$m. If the experiment is carried out in another medium having refractive index 1.2, the fringe width will be _______ $\mu$m.

steps.text: Fringe width $\beta = \lambda D/d$ is proportional to the wavelength.
In a medium of refractive index $\mu$, the wavelength becomes $\lambda' = \lambda/\mu$.

pitfalls: Multiplying by $\mu$ instead of dividing: wavelength shrinks in a denser medium, so fringe width shrinks.
solution.final_check: $\beta' = 2.4/1.2 = 2\,\mu$m: option (B).

subject: physics
stem: A ray of light passing through an equilateral prism has velocity $2.12 \times 10^8$ m/s in the prism material. The minimum angle of deviation is _______ degrees.

pitfalls: Using $v$ directly as $\mu$ instead of $c/v$.
Forgetting that $A = 60^\circ$ for an equilateral prism.
solution.final_check: $\mu \approx \sqrt{2}$ gives $(60+\delta_m)/2 = 45^\circ$: option (B).

subject: physics
stem: A light source having wavelength 331 nm is used to generate photoelectrons whose stopping potential is 0.2 V. The work function of the metal used in the experiment is $\alpha \times 10^{-19}$ J. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.\n($h = 6.62 \times 10^{-34}$ J s, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C and $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s)

pitfalls: Using $\lambda = 331$ nm as $331$ m (unit slip) or forgetting $eV_0$ is in joules already via $e$.
solution.final_check: $\phi = hc/\lambda - eV_0 = (6.0-0.32)\times10^{-19}$ J: option (C).

subject: physics
stem: A compound microscope is designed with two symmetric biconvex lenses. The objective lens is cut vertically, creating two identical plano-convex lenses. One of them is used in place of the original objective lens. To retain the same magnification keeping the object distance unchanged, the tube length has to be _______.

steps.text: Cutting it through the middle gives a plano-convex lens (radii $R, \infty$): $\dfrac{1}{f_0'} = (\mu-1)\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2f_0}$, so $f_0' = 2f_0$; the focal length doubles.
Magnification $m \propto L/f_0$ (object distance, hence $v_0/u_0$, and eyepiece unchanged). To keep $m$ fixed with $f_0' = 2f_0$: $\dfrac{L'}{2f_0} = \dfrac{L}{f_0}$, so $L' = 2L$.
The tube length must be increased two times (doubled).

pitfalls: Cutting 'vertically' here means splitting the biconvex into two plano-convex halves (each keeps one curved face); the power halves, i.e. focal length doubles.
Only the objective changed, so only the $L/f_0$ factor needs compensating.
solution.final_check: $f_0' = 2f_0$ needs $L' = 2L$ for the same $L/f_0$: option (A).

subject: physics
stem: Two wires as shown in the figure below are made of steel and have breaking stress $12 \times 10^8$ N/m$^2$. The area of cross-section of the upper wire is $0.008$ cm$^2$ and of the lower wire is $0.004$ cm$^2$. The maximum mass that can be added to the pan without breaking any wire is _______ kg.\n(take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)\n[Figure: from the ceiling hangs the upper wire, then a 30 kg block, then the lower wire, then a 10 kg block, then the pan.]

steps.text: Maximum force each wire can bear: upper $F_u = 12\times10^8 \times (0.008\times10^{-4}) = 12\times10^8 \times 8\times10^{-7} = 960$ N; lower $F_l = 12\times10^8 \times 4\times10^{-7} = 480$ N.
Let the added pan mass be $m$. Lower wire bears $(10 + m)g$; upper wire bears $(30 + 10 + m)g$.
The lower wire is the binding constraint: $m_{\max} = 38$ kg.

pitfalls: Checking only the upper wire (which bears more load but is also thicker); always test both.
solution.final_check: Lower wire limits $m$ to 38 kg (upper allows 56 kg): option (B).

subject: physics
stem: An a.c. source of angular frequency $\omega$ is connected across a resistor $R$ and a capacitor $C$ in series. The current is observed as $I$. Now the frequency of the source is changed to $\omega/4$ (keeping the voltage unchanged) and the current is found to be $I/3$. The ratio of resistance to reactance at frequency $\omega$ is _______.

pitfalls: At lower frequency the capacitive reactance INCREASES ($X_C \propto 1/\omega$); using $X/4$ instead of $4X$ is the common error.
'Reactance' here means the capacitive reactance $X_C$ at frequency $\omega$.
solution.final_check: $9(R^2+X^2) = R^2+16X^2 \Rightarrow R/X = \sqrt{7/8}$: option (C).

subject: physics
stem: For the given logic circuit, which of the following input combinations will make both LED-1 and LED-2 glow?\n[Figure: inputs A and B feed an OR gate. The OR output drives LED-1 (to ground through a resistor) and also one input of a middle AND gate whose other input is C. The output of the middle AND gate and input A feed a final AND gate, whose output drives LED-2 (to ground through a resistor).]

formulas: LED glows $\iff$ its driving node is HIGH (1)

steps.text: Let $X = A + B$ (OR). LED-1 glows $\iff X = 1$.
Middle AND output: $Y = X \cdot C$. Final AND output: $Z = Y \cdot A = X \cdot C \cdot A$. LED-2 glows $\iff Z = 1$, i.e. $X = 1$, $C = 1$ and $A = 1$.

pitfalls: LED-2 needs $A = 1$ as well (A feeds the final AND directly); options with $A = 0$ can never light LED-2.
solution.final_check: $Z = (A+B)\cdot C\cdot A$ is 1 only for (C): option (C).

subject: physics
stem: A cube has side length 5 cm and modulus of rigidity $10^5$ N/m$^2$. The displacement produced by a force of 10 N in the upper face of the cube is _______ mm.

steps.text: Shear strain $= \Delta x / L$ where $L = 5$ cm $= 0.05$ m is the cube height and $\Delta x$ the top-face displacement.

pitfalls: Using the side length for $A$ as $0.05$ m instead of $A = (0.05)^2$ m$^2$.
Reporting in metres instead of the asked millimetres.

subject: physics
stem: From 18 m height above the ground a ball is dropped from rest. The height above the ground at which the magnitude of velocity equals the magnitude of acceleration (in the same set of units) due to gravity is _______ m.\n(Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$ and neglect air resistance.)

steps.text: Numerically $|v| = |g| = 10$, so $v = 10$ m/s at the required point.
If the ball has fallen a distance $S$, $v^2 = 2gS$, i.e. $100 = 2 \times 10 \times S$, so $S = 5$ m.

pitfalls: Setting $v = g$ dimensionally is only a numerical equality — the question explicitly says 'in the same set of units', so just equate the numbers.
Answering the fallen distance (5 m) instead of the height above ground (13 m).
solution.final_check: $v^2 = 2g(18-h) = 100 \Rightarrow 18-h = 5 \Rightarrow h = 13$ m.

subject: physics
stem: A transverse wave on a string is described by $y = 3\sin(36t + 0.018x + \pi/4)$, where $x, y$ are in cm and $t$ in seconds. The least distance between two successive crests in the wave is _______ cm. (Nearest integer)\n($\pi = 3.14$)

steps.text: Comparing with $y = A\sin(\omega t + kx + \phi_0)$: wave number $k = 0.018$ rad/cm.
Successive crests are one wavelength apart: $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14}{0.018} = \dfrac{6.28}{0.018} = 348.89$ cm.

pitfalls: Reading the coefficient of $t$ (36) as the wave number; $k$ is the coefficient of $x$.
Forgetting the 'nearest integer' instruction.
solution.final_check: $\lambda = 2\pi/0.018 = 348.89 \approx 349$ cm.

subject: physics
stem: A charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field of $(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$ T has an acceleration $\left(4\hat{i} - \dfrac{x}{2}\hat{j}\right)$ m/s$^2$. The value of $x$ is _______.

steps.text: The magnetic force (hence acceleration) is always perpendicular to the magnetic field: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{B} = 0$.

pitfalls: Trying to use $\vec{v}$ (not given) instead of the perpendicularity condition, which needs no velocity at all.
Sign slip in the dot product.
solution.final_check: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{B} = 12 - x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 12$.

subject: physics
stem: In the given circuit below, inductance values of $L_1$, $L_2$ and $L_3$ are the same. The magnetic energy stored in the entire circuit is ($U_t$) and that stored in the $L_2$ inductor is ($U_l$). $U_t/U_l$ is _______.\n(Ignore the mutual inductance, if any.)\n[Figure: current enters from the left and passes through $L_1$, then splits into two parallel branches — $L_2$ on top and $L_3$ below — which recombine and exit to the right. All three inductances are equal.]

formulas: Equal parallel inductors split current equally

steps.text: Let each inductance be $L$ and the total current through $L_1$ be $I$.
$L_2$ and $L_3$ are in parallel with equal inductance, so the current splits equally: $I/2$ through each.

pitfalls: Forgetting that energy goes as $I^2$: the parallel branches each store $1/4$ (not $1/2$) of $\tfrac{1}{2}LI^2$.
Treating $L_2, L_3$ as series instead of parallel.
solution.final_check: $U_t = \tfrac{3}{4}LI^2$, $U_l = \tfrac{1}{8}LI^2$, ratio $6$.

subject: chemistry
stem:
How many grams of residue is obtained by heating 2.76 g of silver carbonate?
(Given: Molar mass of C, O and Ag are 12, 16 and 108 g mol$^{-1}$ respectively)

steps.text: On heating, silver carbonate decomposes completely to silver metal (the residue), carbon dioxide and oxygen: $\ce{2Ag2CO3 -> 4Ag + 2CO2 + O2}$.
From the balanced equation, 2 mol $\ce{Ag2CO3}$ give 4 mol Ag, so 0.01 mol gives 0.02 mol Ag. Mass of residue $= 0.02 \times 108 = 2.16$ g.

pitfalls: Assuming the residue is $\ce{Ag2O}$ (2.32 g) — on strong heating $\ce{Ag2O}$ itself decomposes to Ag metal.
Missing the 2:4 stoichiometric ratio between $\ce{Ag2CO3}$ and Ag.
solution.final_check: 2.16 g of Ag from 2.76 g of $\ce{Ag2CO3}$ balances mass with the evolved $\ce{CO2}$ + $\ce{O2}$; matches option B.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Arrange the following atomic orbitals of multi electron atoms in order of increasing energy.
A. $n = 3, l = 2, m = +1$
B. $n = 4, l = 0, m = 0$
C. $n = 6, l = 1, m = 0$
D. $n = 5, l = 1, m = +1$
E. $n = 2, l = 1, m = +1$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

formulas: Orbital energy increases with $(n+l)$; for equal $(n+l)$, lower $n$ has lower energy.

steps.text: Identify each orbital: A = 3d, B = 4s, C = 6p, D = 5p, E = 2p.
Increasing energy: E(3) < B(4) < A(5) < D(6) < C(7), i.e. E < B < A < D < C.

pitfalls: Using only $n$ (wrong for multi-electron atoms) or only $l$ to order the orbitals.
solution.final_check: Option D lists exactly E < B < A < D < C, the $(n+l)$ order computed above.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Identify the **correct** statements from the following:
A. Heisenberg uncertainty principle is applicable to electrons.
B. The size of 2p$_x$ orbital is less than the size of 3p$_x$ orbital.
C. The energy of 2s orbital of H atom is equal to the energy of 2s orbital of Li.
D. The electronic configuration of Cr is [Ar] 3d$^5$ 4s$^1$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

steps.text: A is correct: the uncertainty principle applies to microscopic particles such as electrons.
B is correct: orbital size grows with principal quantum number, so 2p$_x$ < 3p$_x$.
C is incorrect: neutral Li is a multi-electron atom, so its 2s energy is not the hydrogenic $-13.6/4$ eV value of the H atom.
D is correct: Cr has the anomalous half-filled configuration [Ar] 3d$^5$ 4s$^1$. Hence A, B and D only.

pitfalls: Treating neutral Li as hydrogen-like when comparing orbital energies.
Writing Cr as [Ar] 3d$^4$ 4s$^2$ instead of the stable half-filled 3d$^5$ 4s$^1$.
solution.final_check: Three statements verified true (A, B, D) and C refuted on multi-electron grounds; option B is the only match.

What is the mole fraction of water in 10% by weight (w/w) of aqueous urea solution?
[Given: Molar mass of H, O, C and N are 1, 16, 12 and 14 g mol$^{-1}$ respectively.]

steps.text: In 100 g of 10% (w/w) solution: 10 g urea and 90 g water.
Moles of urea $= 10/60 = 1/6 \approx 0.1667$; moles of water $= 90/18 = 5$.

pitfalls: Using mass ratio instead of mole ratio, or computing the mole fraction of urea (0.032) instead of water.
solution.final_check: 30/31 = 0.9677 rounds to the listed 0.967 (option D); the complement 0.032 is option B, the urea fraction.

stem: M$_3$A$_2$ is a sparingly soluble salt of molar mass $y$ g mol$^{-1}$ and solubility $x$ g L$^{-1}$. The ratio of the molar concentration of the anion (A$^{3-}$) to the solubility product of the salt is

steps.text: Molar solubility $S = x/y$ mol L$^{-1}$; anion concentration $[\ce{A^{3-}}] = 2S = 2x/y$.

pitfalls: Writing $K_{sp} = 6S^5$ by forgetting the stoichiometric powers 3 and 2.
Using solubility $x$ directly in mol L$^{-1}$ without dividing by molar mass $y$.
solution.final_check: Dimensional check: ratio has units of (mol L$^{-1}$)$^{-4}$, matching $y^4/x^4$; option A is the exact derived form.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Arrange the following resultant mixtures in increasing order of their pH values
A. 10 mL 0.2 M Ca(OH)$_2$ + 25 mL 0.1 M HCl
B. 10 mL 0.01 M H$_2$SO$_4$ + 10 mL 0.01 M Ca(OH)$_2$
C. 10 mL 0.1 M H$_2$SO$_4$ + 10 mL 0.1 M KOH
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

formulas: millimoles of H$^+$ or OH$^-$ $= 2 \times V(\text{mL}) \times M$ for diprotic $\ce{H2SO4}$/$\ce{Ca(OH)2}$

steps.text: A: OH$^-$ $= 2 \times 10 \times 0.2 = 4$ mmol; H$^+$ $= 25 \times 0.1 = 2.5$ mmol $\rightarrow$ excess OH$^-$ (1.5 mmol/35 mL), basic, highest pH.
B: H$^+$ $= 2 \times 10 \times 0.01 = 0.2$ mmol; OH$^-$ $= 2 \times 10 \times 0.01 = 0.2$ mmol $\rightarrow$ exactly neutral, pH = 7.
C: H$^+$ $= 2 \times 10 \times 0.1 = 2$ mmol; OH$^-$ $= 10 \times 0.1 = 1$ mmol $\rightarrow$ excess H$^+$ (1 mmol/20 mL = 0.05 M), acidic, lowest pH. Order: C < B < A.

pitfalls: Forgetting the factor of 2 for the diprotic acid $\ce{H2SO4}$ and diacidic base $\ce{Ca(OH)2}$.
Comparing molarities instead of total millimoles of H$^+$/OH$^-$.
solution.final_check: C is the only acidic mixture, B is exactly neutral, A is the only basic one — C < B < A (option C) is forced.

subject: chemistry
stem:
First order gas phase reaction
A $\rightarrow$ B + C
$p_i$ = initial pressure of gas A, $p_t$ = total pressure of the reaction mixture at time $t$
Expression of rate constant ($k$) is

steps.text: Let $x$ be the fall in pressure of A at time $t$: $p_A = p_i - x$, $p_B = p_C = x$. Total pressure $p_t = (p_i - x) + x + x = p_i + x$, so $x = p_t - p_i$.

pitfalls: Using $p_t - p_i$ as the remaining pressure of A instead of $2p_i - p_t$.
Applying the $\ce{A -> 2B}$-type formula $p_i/(2p_i - p_t)$ blindly is actually correct here — but only because the stoichiometry gives the same total-pressure relation; derive it fresh each time.
solution.final_check: At $t = 0$, $p_t = p_i$ gives $\ln(1) = 0$ as required, and $p_t \to 2p_i$ (complete reaction) gives $p_A \to 0$; option A satisfies both limits.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Given below are two statements:
**Statement I:** The correct order of electronegativity of fluorine, oxygen and nitrogen is F > O > N.
**Statement II:** The oxidation state of oxygen in OF$_2$ is +2 and in Na$_2$O is $-$2.
In the light of the above statements, choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

formulas: Electronegativity decreases down a group and increases across a period: F > O > N.
Oxidation state = charge assuming the more electronegative atom takes the shared electrons.

steps.text: Statement I is true: Pauling electronegativities F (4.0) > O (3.5) > N (3.0).
Statement II is true: in $\ce{OF2}$ fluorine is more electronegative, so O is +2; in $\ce{Na2O}$ oxygen is more electronegative than Na, so O is $-$2.

pitfalls: Assigning oxygen $-$2 in $\ce{OF2}$ by habit — fluorine outranks oxygen in electronegativity.
Doubting F > O > N because nitrogen has a half-filled shell (that affects electron affinity trends, not this order).
solution.final_check: Both statements check out independently against standard data; option A.

subject: chemistry
stem:
**Correct** statements from the following are:
A. Nitrogen in oxidation states from +1 to +4 disproportionates in acid medium.
B. Nitrogen has the ability to form d$\pi$–p$\pi$ multiple bonds with itself and other elements with small size and high electronegativity.
C. N–N single bond is stronger than P–P single bond.
D. Nitrogen has highest density in its group due to small size.
E. The maximum covalency of nitrogen is four since it has only four valence orbitals for bonding.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

steps.text: A is correct: nitrogen species in +1 to +4 oxidation states (e.g. $\ce{HNO2}$) disproportionate in acidic medium.
B is incorrect: nitrogen has no d-orbitals in its valence shell; it forms p$\pi$–p$\pi$ multiple bonds, not d$\pi$–p$\pi$.
C is incorrect: lone-pair repulsion in the small N atom makes the N–N single bond weaker than P–P.
D is incorrect: density increases down group 15; nitrogen has the lowest density.
E is correct: with only 2s + 2p valence orbitals and no d-orbitals, nitrogen's maximum covalency is 4. Hence A and E only.

pitfalls: Confusing nitrogen's p$\pi$–p$\pi$ bonding with the d$\pi$–p$\pi$ bonding of heavier congeners like phosphorus.
Assuming small size always means stronger bonds (ignores lone-pair repulsion in N–N).
solution.final_check: Exactly two statements survive scrutiny (A, E); option D is the only pair matching.

subject: chemistry
stem: Which of the following is **NOT** a physical or chemical characteristics of interstitial compounds?

options.A: They have high melting points, higher than those of pure metals.
options.B: They are very soft and ionic in nature.
options.D: They are chemically inert and usually non-stoichiometric.

formulas: Interstitial compounds: small atoms (H, C, N, B) trapped in metal lattice voids.

steps.text: A is a true characteristic: interstitial compounds have very high melting points, above those of the pure metals.
C is a true characteristic: they retain metallic conductivity.
D is a true characteristic: they are chemically inert and typically non-stoichiometric.
B is NOT a characteristic: interstitial compounds are very hard (not soft) and retain metallic character (not ionic).

pitfalls: Confusing interstitial compounds with ionic hydrides/carbides.
Missing the NOT in the question and picking a true characteristic.
solution.final_check: B contradicts the defining hardness and metallic nature of interstitial compounds; all other options are textbook characteristics.

subject: chemistry
stem:
The **correct** statements about metal carbonyls are
A. The metal-carbon bonds in metal carbonyls possess both $\sigma$ and $\pi$-character.
B. Due to synergic bonding interactions between metal and CO ligand, the metal-carbon bond becomes weak.
C. The metal-carbon $\sigma$ bond is formed by the donation of lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of metal.
D. The metal-carbon $\pi$ bond is formed by the donation of electrons from filled d-orbital of metal into vacant $\pi^*$ orbital of CO.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

formulas: M–C $\sigma$: C(lone pair) $\rightarrow$ M(vacant); M–C $\pi$: M(filled d) $\rightarrow$ CO($\pi^*$), back-bonding.

steps.text: A is correct: the M–C bond has $\sigma$ (donation) plus $\pi$ (back-donation) character.
B is incorrect: synergic bonding strengthens (shortens) the M–C bond; it is the C–O bond that weakens.
C is correct: $\sigma$ donation of the carbon lone pair into a vacant metal orbital.
D is correct: $\pi$ back-donation from filled metal d-orbitals into the vacant $\pi^*$ orbital of CO. Hence A, C and D.

pitfalls: Thinking synergic effect weakens the M–C bond — it weakens C–O and strengthens M–C.
Reversing the direction of $\sigma$ donation (metal to carbon).
solution.final_check: A, C, D are the standard synergic-bonding description; B inverts the effect; option B matches.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Given below are two statements:
**Statement I:** Each electron in e$_g$ orbitals destabilizes the orbitals by +0.6 $\Delta_o$ and each electron in the t$_{2g}$ orbitals stabilizes the orbitals by –0.4 $\Delta_o$ in an octahedral field on the basis of crystal field theory.
**Statement II:** All the d-orbitals of the transition metals have the same energy in their free atomic state but when a complex is formed the ligands destroy the degeneracy of these orbitals on the basis of crystal field theory.
In the light of the above statements, choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
options.C: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
options.D: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

steps.text: Statement I is correct: relative to the barycentre, t$_{2g}$ lies 0.4$\Delta_o$ lower and e$_g$ lies 0.6$\Delta_o$ higher per electron.
Statement II is correct: the five d-orbitals are degenerate in the free ion; the ligand field splits them (t$_{2g}$/e$_g$ in octahedral) — the core premise of CFT.

pitfalls: Mixing up the signs (t$_{2g}$ is stabilized, $-$0.4; e$_g$ is destabilized, +0.6).
Confusing crystal field splitting with the spectrochemical series ordering of ligands.
solution.final_check: Both statements are verbatim CFT fundamentals; option A.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Given below are two statements:
**Statement I:** On the basis of inductive effect, the order of stability of alkyl carbanions is CH$_3^-$ > CH$_3$–CH$_2^-$ > (CH$_3$)$_2$CH$^-$ > (CH$_3$)$_3$C$^-$.
**Statement II:** Allyl and benzyl carbanions are more stabilised by inductive effect and not by resonance effect.
In the light of the above statements, choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
options.C: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
options.D: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

formulas: Alkyl groups exert +I effect, destabilizing a carbanion: more alkyl $\rightarrow$ less stable carbanion.

steps.text: Statement I is correct: electron-donating alkyl groups intensify the negative charge, so stability falls CH$_3^-$ > 1$^\circ$ > 2$^\circ$ > 3$^\circ$ (opposite of carbocations).
Statement II is incorrect: allyl and benzyl carbanions are stabilized by resonance delocalization of the negative charge (conjugation with the $\pi$ system), not by the inductive effect.
Thus Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

pitfalls: Applying the carbocation stability order (3$^\circ$ > 2$^\circ$ > 1$^\circ$) to carbanions — it is reversed.
Attributing allyl/benzyl anion stability to +I of alkyl/aryl groups instead of resonance.
solution.final_check: The two statements test opposite effects (+I vs resonance); only I survives — option C.

subject: chemistry
stem:
"P" is a hydrocarbon of molecular formula C$_8$H$_{14}$. On ozonolysis, "P" forms "Q". "Q" on treatment with alkali under reflux condition produces "R", which on treatment with I$_2$/NaOH gives a yellow precipitate. Acidification of the solution gives "S". The structure of "S" is 2-methylcyclopent-1-ene-1-carboxylic acid (a five-membered ring with the C=C between the carbon bearing –COOH and the carbon bearing –CH$_3$).
The correct structure of "P" is

options.A: Cyclohexene ring with a –CH$_3$ on each of the two ring carbons farthest from the C=C (dimethylcyclohexene, methyls not on the double bond)
options.C: 1-Ethyl-2-methylcyclopent-1-ene (cyclopentene with –CH$_3$ on one and –CH$_2$CH$_3$ on the other doubly-bonded carbon)

formulas: Ozonolysis of cyclic alkene $\rightarrow$ dicarbonyl (ring opens, C count kept).

steps.text: Work backward from S: the yellow precipitate with $\ce{I2}$/NaOH is iodoform, so R contains $\ce{CH3CO-}$; acidification gives R$'$COOH = S, hence R = 1-acetyl-2-methylcyclopent-1-ene.

R (5-membered enone-free alkene with exocyclic acetyl) comes from intramolecular aldol condensation of a C$_8$ 1,4-diketone Q: enolate of octane-2,7-dione ($\ce{CH3COCH2CH2CH2CH2COCH3}$) attacks the far carbonyl, closing a 5-membered ring and dehydrating to the observed alkene.
Q = octane-2,7-dione is exactly the ozonolysis product of 1,2-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene (ring opens at C1=C2, each substituted sp$^2$ carbon becoming $\ce{CH3CO-}$).

The other options fail: (A) gives a dialdehyde (no acetyl, iodoform negative); (B) gives 6-oxooctanal $\rightarrow$ propionyl product (iodoform negative); (C) gives octane-2,6-dione $\rightarrow$ 6-membered aldol product.

pitfalls: Assuming any cyclic alkene works — the iodoform test demands a surviving $\ce{CH3CO-}$ group, which only the 1,2-dimethyl case supplies after aldol cyclization.
Forming a 6-membered ring from octane-2,6-dione (option C) — check ring size for each enolate/electrophile pair.
solution.final_check: Only 1,2-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene traces forward through ozonolysis $\rightarrow$ aldol $\rightarrow$ haloform to the given S; option D.

subject: chemistry
stem:
For the following Friedel Craft's alkylation reaction, which of the statements are **correct**?
Benzene + CH$_3$CH$_2$CH$_2$Cl $\xrightarrow[\text{Anhydrous}]{\text{AlCl}_3}$ Alkylbenzene
A. Major product is n-propyl benzene.
B. iso-propyl carbocation intermediate is also generated.
C. Multiple substitution is inevitable.
D. Introducing electron-donating substituent on benzene will not produce any alkyl benzene.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

steps.text: A is incorrect: the primary n-propyl carbocation rearranges by hydride shift to the more stable isopropyl carbocation, so the major product is isopropylbenzene (cumene), not n-propylbenzene.
B is correct: the isopropyl (2$^\circ$) carbocation is generated via the rearrangement.
C is correct: the alkyl group activates the ring toward further electrophilic substitution, so polyalkylation accompanies F–C alkylation (a known limitation).
D is incorrect: electron-donating groups activate the ring and favour F–C alkylation. Hence B and C only.

pitfalls: Forgetting carbocation rearrangement in F–C alkylation with primary halides of 3+ carbons.
Thinking an activating group deactivates the ring toward electrophilic substitution.
solution.final_check: B and C are the two textbook-correct statements; option B.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Benzyl isocyanide can be obtained from
A. C$_6$H$_5$CH$_2$Br $\xrightarrow{\text{AgCN}}$
B. C$_6$H$_5$CH$_2$NH$_2$ $\xrightarrow[\text{Aq. NaOH}]{\text{CHCl}_3}$
C. C$_6$H$_5$Br $\xrightarrow{\text{AgCN}}$
D. C$_6$H$_5$NH$_2$ $\xrightarrow[\text{Aq. NaOH}]{\text{CHCl}_3}$
E. C$_6$H$_5$CH$_2$CH$_2$Br $\xrightarrow{\text{KCN}}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

steps.text: A is correct: benzyl bromide + AgCN gives benzyl isocyanide ($\ce{C6H5CH2NC}$) via N-attack of the ambident cyanide.
B is correct: benzylamine undergoes the carbylamine reaction to give benzyl isocyanide.
C gives phenyl isocyanide ($\ce{C6H5NC}$), not benzyl isocyanide.
D gives phenyl isocyanide, not benzyl isocyanide.
E gives the nitrile $\ce{C6H5CH2CH2CN}$ (KCN attacks through carbon), not an isocyanide. Hence A and B only.

pitfalls: Mixing up AgCN (isocyanide) and KCN (nitrile) products.
Missing that C and D give the phenyl, not benzyl, isocyanide.
solution.final_check: Only A and B deliver the benzyl ($\ce{C6H5CH2-}$) skeleton as the isocyanide; option A.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Consider compounds A, B and C with following structural formulae
A = CH$_3$–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–OH
B = CH$_2$=CH–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–CH$_3$
C = HO–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–CH(OH)–CH$_3$
For the conversion of B from A, reagent (D) required is ______ and structural formula of product (E) obtained when C undergoes same reaction using excess reagent (D) is ______.

options.D: D = Conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ or H$_3$PO$_4$; E = CH$_2$=CH–CH=CH$_2$

steps.text: A (pentan-1-ol) $\rightarrow$ B (pent-1-ene) is an acid-catalyzed dehydration, so D = conc. $\ce{H2SO4}$ (PCC is an oxidant, not a dehydrating agent).
C is butane-1,3-diol; with excess dehydrating acid both –OH groups eliminate: first the secondary OH (Saytzeff) then the primary, giving the conjugated diene buta-1,3-diene $\ce{CH2=CH-CH=CH2}$.
Only option D pairs conc. $\ce{H2SO4}$/$\ce{H3PO4}$ with butadiene as E.

pitfalls: Choosing PCC (an oxidizer to carbonyls) for a dehydration.
Stopping at mono-dehydration of the diol despite 'excess reagent'.
solution.final_check: Dehydration needs acid (not PCC), and excess acid doubly dehydrates the 1,3-diol to butadiene — option D.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Identify the **incorrect** statements.
A. Benzylamine (C$_6$H$_5$CH$_2$NH$_2$) is a stronger base than aniline (C$_6$H$_5$NH$_2$).
B. p-Anisidine (4-CH$_3$O–C$_6$H$_4$–NH$_2$) can be synthesized by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
C. C$_6$H$_5$CH$_2$CONH$_2$ $\xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2, \text{NaOH}}$ primary aromatic amine
D. p-Nitroaniline $\xrightarrow[\text{(ii) } \Delta]{\text{(i) NaNO}_2, \text{ HCl}, 0^\circ\text{C}}$ product will dissolve in NaOH
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

formulas: Gabriel synthesis works only for aliphatic primary amines (aryl halides do not undergo SN2).

steps.text: A is correct: in benzylamine the nitrogen lone pair is not delocalized into the ring (CH$_2$ spacer), so it is more basic than aniline.
B is incorrect: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis cannot make aromatic amines since aryl halides do not undergo the required nucleophilic substitution.
C is incorrect: Hofmann degradation of $\ce{C6H5CH2CONH2}$ gives $\ce{C6H5CH2NH2}$ (benzylamine), in which $\ce{-NH2}$ is not directly on the ring — not a primary aromatic amine.
D is correct: diazotization followed by heating hydrolyzes the diazonium salt to p-nitrophenol, which dissolves in NaOH. Incorrect statements: B and C.

pitfalls: Calling benzylamine an aromatic amine — the $\ce{-NH2}$ must be directly attached to the ring.
Forgetting that the Hofmann product has one carbon fewer than the amide.
solution.final_check: B and C are the two false statements; option C.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Identify the **correct** statements.
A. Glucose exists in two anomeric forms.
B. Anomers of glucose differ in configuration at C–1 in cyclic hemiacetal structure.
C. Melting point of $\alpha$-anomer of glucose is greater than $\beta$-anomer.
D. Specific rotation of $\alpha$-anomer is +19$^\circ$ while for $\beta$-anomer is +112$^\circ$.
E. $\alpha$ and $\beta$-anomers of glucose are prepared by crystallization of saturated glucose solution at 303 K and 371 K respectively.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

formulas: Anomers: differ only in configuration at the anomeric carbon (C-1).

steps.text: A is correct: glucose exists as $\alpha$ and $\beta$ anomers.
B is correct: anomers differ in configuration at C-1 of the cyclic hemiacetal.
C is incorrect: mp($\alpha$) = 419 K < mp($\beta$) = 423 K.
D is incorrect: the rotations are swapped — $[\alpha]_D$ is +112$^\circ$ for $\alpha$ and +19$^\circ$ for $\beta$.
E is correct: $\alpha$ crystallizes at 303 K and $\beta$ at 371 K. Hence A, B and E.

pitfalls: Swapping the $\alpha$/$\beta$ values of specific rotation or melting point.
Confusing anomers (C-1) with epimers (any single stereocenter).
solution.final_check: A, B, E verified true while C and D invert known data; option D.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Given below are two statements:
**Statement I:** Sodium dichromate and potassium dichromate are classified as primary standards in titrimetric analysis.
**Statement II:** Phenolphthalein is a weak base, therefore it dissociates in acidic medium.
In the light of the above statements, choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

formulas: Primary standard: pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, high molar mass (e.g. $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$).
Phenolphthalein: weak acid $\ce{HPh <=> H+ + Ph^-}$ (colourless $\rightleftharpoons$ pink).

steps.text: Statement I is false: potassium dichromate is a primary standard, but sodium dichromate is hygroscopic/deliquescent and is not one — the statement claims both are.
Statement II is false: phenolphthalein is a weak acid, not a weak base.

pitfalls: Assuming sodium dichromate shares potassium dichromate's primary-standard status.
Misremembering phenolphthalein as a weak base.
solution.final_check: Each statement contains one factual inversion; both are false — option B.

subject: chemistry
stem:
Consider the following species:
BrF$_5$, XeF$_5^-$, BF$_4^-$, ICl$_4^-$, XeF$_4$, SF$_4$, NH$_4^+$, ClF$_3$, XeF$_2$, ICl$_2^-$
Number of species having sp$^3$d hybridized central atom is ______.

formulas: Steric number $= \sigma$-bonds + lone pairs; sp$^3$d $\iff$ steric number $= 5$.

steps.text: Count electron domains on the central atom: BrF$_5$ (6, sp$^3$d$^2$), XeF$_5^-$ (7, sp$^3$d$^3$), BF$_4^-$ (4, sp$^3$), ICl$_4^-$ (6, sp$^3$d$^2$), XeF$_4$ (6, sp$^3$d$^2$) — none sp$^3$d.
SF$_4$: 4 bonds + 1 lone pair = 5 $\rightarrow$ sp$^3$d. NH$_4^+$: 4 $\rightarrow$ sp$^3$. ClF$_3$: 3 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 5 $\rightarrow$ sp$^3$d.
XeF$_2$: 2 bonds + 3 lone pairs = 5 $\rightarrow$ sp$^3$d. ICl$_2^-$: 2 bonds + 3 lone pairs = 5 $\rightarrow$ sp$^3$d.
sp$^3$d species: SF$_4$, ClF$_3$, XeF$_2$, ICl$_2^-$ — a total of 4.

pitfalls: Forgetting the extra electron from the negative charge when counting lone pairs (XeF$_5^-$, ICl$_4^-$, ICl$_2^-$).
Assigning sp$^3$d to XeF$_4$/BrF$_5$ (steric number 6 $\rightarrow$ sp$^3$d$^2$).
solution.final_check: 4 species have steric number exactly 5; the rest are 4, 6 or 7.

subject: chemistry
stem:
In an estimation of sulphur by Carius method 0.2 g of the substance gave 0.6 g of BaSO$_4$. The percentage of sulphur in the substance is ______ %.
(Given molar mass in g mol$^{-1}$ S: 32, BaSO$_4$: 231)

steps.text: All sulphur precipitates as $\ce{BaSO4}$: 32 g S $\equiv$ 231 g $\ce{BaSO4}$.

pitfalls: Using the actual molar mass 233.4 instead of the given 231.
Forgetting the $\times 100$ for percentage.
solution.final_check: 41.56% rounds to 42, the nearest integer.

subject: chemistry
stem:
One mole of phenol is treated with dilute HNO$_3$ at 298 K to give a mixture of products. The mixture is separated by steam distillation. The steam volatile compound (X) is separated. The increase in percentage of oxygen in (X) with respect to phenol is ______ $\times 10^{-1}$ %
(Given molar mass in g mol$^{-1}$ H:1, C:12, N:14, O:16)

steps.text: Dilute $\ce{HNO3}$ at 298 K nitrates phenol to o- and p-nitrophenol; the steam-volatile isomer is o-nitrophenol (intramolecular H-bonding), so X = o-nitrophenol, $\ce{C6H5NO3}$, M = 139.

pitfalls: Using p-nitrophenol (same formula — no error here, but picking the non-volatile isomer misreads the separation).
Reporting the absolute %O of X instead of the increase over phenol.
solution.final_check: 17.51% = 175.1 × 10⁻¹%, nearest integer 175.

subject: chemistry
stem:
The values of pressure equilibrium constant recorded at different temperatures for the following equilibrium reaction have been given below
A(g) $\rightleftharpoons$ B(g) + C(g)

| 1/T (K$^{-1}$) | log$_{10}$K$_p$ |
| 0.05 | 3.5 |
| 0.06 | 2.5 |
| 0.07 | 1.5 |

The magnitude of $\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}$ calculated from the above data is ______. (Nearest integer)

pitfalls: Dropping the 2.303 factor (using ln $K_p$ slope directly) or taking the slope as positive.
Sign error: $K_p$ falls as $1/T$ rises, so $\Delta H^\circ$ is positive (endothermic).
solution.final_check: Slope −100 × 2.303 = 230.3 → 230; consistent across all three data pairs.

stem:
If the half life of a first order reaction is 6.93 minutes then the time required for completion of 99% of the reaction will be ______ minutes.
(Given: log 2 = 0.3010)

pitfalls: Using $t_{99\%} = 2 \times t_{1/2}$ (that gives 75%, not 99%).
Mixing log and ln in the integrated rate law.

stem: Consider the system of linear equations in $x, y, z$: $x + 2y + tz = 0$, $6x + y + 5tz = 0$, $3x + t^2y + f(t)z = 0$, where $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a differentiable function. If this system has infinitely many solutions for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f$

formulas: Homogeneous system has non-trivial (hence infinitely many) solutions $\iff \det = 0$

steps.text: For infinitely many solutions for every $t$, $\Delta(t)=\begin{vmatrix}1&2&t\\6&1&5t\\3&t^2&f(t)\end{vmatrix}=0$ for all $t$.
$f'(t) = \dfrac{3t^2+27}{11} > 0$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ (discriminant $0-4\cdot3\cdot27<0$), so $f$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting that a homogeneous system with $\det=0$ automatically has infinitely many solutions.
Concluding only $f'\ge 0$ without checking it never vanishes.
solution.final_check: $f(t)=(t^3+27t)/11$ has $f'(t)>0$ everywhere, so option B.

Forgetting the $\pi/4$ cancels.

Then the number of integral values of $p$, for which the equation $x^2 + y^2 - 2px + 2py + \alpha + 2 = 0$ represents a circle of radius $r \le 6$, is ______.

steps.text: Put $y=vx$: $x\sin v\,(v\,dx+x\,dv)=(vx\sin v-x)dx\Rightarrow x\sin v\,dv=-dx\Rightarrow \sin v\,dv=-\frac{dx}{x}$.
Integrating: $-\cos v=-\ln x+C$. $y(1)=\frac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow v(1)=\frac{\pi}{2}$: $0=0+C\Rightarrow C=0$. So $\cos\frac{y}{x}=\ln x$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the reality condition $r^2>0$ (excludes $p^2=7$ region edge).
Sign error: constant term is $\alpha+2=14$, subtracted in $r^2$.
